item.title: They Watched Me for Fourteen Months, Then Someone Saw Me
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

They Watched Me for Fourteen Months, Then Someone Saw Me

Personal Perspective: The difference between being observed and being known.

Posted August 19, 2026

Key points
  • Surveillance classifies and predicts; witnessing seeks to know another person.
  • Limbic resonance is the biological basis of therapeutic connection.
  • The therapeutic alliance predicts outcomes better than any specific method.
  • Medication can stabilize a brain; only recognition can make it worth inhabiting.
Source: Quang Nguyen Vinh/Pexels

The very same day I was discharged from the state psychiatric hospital where I spent nearly a year as a patient, I walked directly into my new therapist's office. The State, with a genius for bureaucratic timing, delayed my release by a day and fused two monumental events into one. I arrived wearing a GPS ankle monitor affixed to my left leg, the latest link in an unbroken chain of institutional surveillance.

What I discovered was a space constructed by someone who believed the unconscious deserved a home worthy of it. Every surface was adorned. In the wake of 14 months of cinderblock and flat institutional light, it was less overwhelming than dislocating, as if I had walked into a heated house after an arduous trek in a snowstorm. I found a seat on an immaculate white couch and caught the comforting gaze of the woman across from me.

Susan was in her seventies, and she wore clothing that announced a protest of the mundane. Colorful and overgrown, in the way a garden can be when someone has loved it past the point of tidiness and embraced the wildness as a more honest expression of truth.

From the first session, Susan lent me what psychoanalyst Theodor Reik dubbed the third ear; the way of listening to another that is attuned not only to the content of speech but to the hidden messages beneath the words.

I had long been silencing those hidden frequencies. The grief around my father's death that I buried. The shame of my failure as an intellectual. The relational world of family and friends that bipolar disorder had systematically dismantled. In the place of social connection, mania gave me the certainty that I was a sufficient world unto myself. Depression joined with substance abuse to cut me off from the possibility of love. Whether up or down, the illness performed the same brutal act: it severed me from the world.

But in that ornately decorated room, Susan made me feel seen. She asked me about my gym sessions, about my mother, and about my values. A few months in, she asked to read the psychiatric reports from the state hospital, and she returned visibly moved by the gap between the manic man she read about in the bureaucratic lexicon of danger and threat and the man now sitting across from her. When she asked about my father's death from Parkinson's, about how I was absent from his life when he died, she let the gap between my words fill the room. She shared her intimate connection to mental illness: what it meant to watch a brother consumed by schizoaffective illness in a psychiatric hospital where he eventually died. That experience had clearly weighed on her, but she shared it in the spirit of empathy rather than seeking credit.

She also opened her door to my mother—something the state hospital never had a mechanism for. Recognition, Susan understood, must not be private. It should be communal.

Source: Matthew Henry/StockSnap

Surveillance and Witnessing

I have reflected before about a hospital that kept me safe but never knew me, and about a psychiatrist whose fifteen-minute med checks could manage my lithium level without ever asking me a personal question. Susan provided a counterbalance to both.

Michel Foucault wrote that the genius of the modern institution is not its overt cruelty but its totalizing gaze: the person being watched internalizes the watching and becomes his own overseer. I had spent 14 months molding myself to that gaze, assimilated not only by cameras and medication logs but by the very knowledge of their presence. Make no mistake: all of it had been, in its administrative way, conscientious and diligent. But few institutional observers were interested in my subjective personhood—what it feels like to be a prisoner or a patient.

On the surface, surveillance and witnessing have similarities. Both direct attention your way. But the difference is found in their operating rationale: while surveillance seeks to classify, predict, and warn, witnessing seeks to know another human being.

In A General Theory of Love, psychiatrists Thomas Lewis, Fari Amini, and Richard Lannon provided me with a vocabulary for the difference in care. When Susan witnessed me, she provided me with limbic resonance: a neurobiological process by which two nervous systems become attuned to each other's interior states.

During my decade of illness, I lived in the absence of sustained resonance. The manic mind is unusually resistant to attunement, operating with the conviction that its certainty is a world sufficient to itself. In contrast, Susan offered, in session after session, the gifts of attunement and witnessing, necessary corrections after a long interpersonal exile. Lewis, Amini, and Lannon observe that the goal of therapy is to listen as a means of being present for another, to recognize their humanity. And Susan listened with her body as much as her mind. After years of professional observation, her office was the first place where the recognition itself felt like medicine.

What Medication Cannot Reach

As much as attunement matters, it would be misleading to suggest that connection alone heals mental illness. The lithium I take is effective; the diagnosis and the pharmacological calibration are crucial. But they are not sufficient. Dean Ornish, reviewing decades of medical evidence, concluded that if a pharmaceutical drug had the same positive outcomes as love and social connection, every doctor in the country would prescribe it. No one does, because there is no patent on presence. Only the experience of being seen, known, and recognized can rebuild what illness dismantles: not the neural circuitry, which medication addresses, but the self's sense of its own belonging in the human world.

Jerome Frank's and Kay Redfield Jamison's work confirms that the theoretical orientation of therapy—whether CBT or psychodynamic—is of far less importance than the quality of the patient-therapist bond, the therapeutic alliance.

After months of being surveilled, what I needed was not a method. I needed Susan's third ear. And somewhere in the patient listening—in the limbic resonance of two people sitting together long enough for the signal to find its frequency—the part of me that had been speaking into silence for years began, gradually, to hear itself answered.

In the hospital, I had been observed. In Susan's office, I was recognized. That distinction is the whole of the medicine that medication cannot reach.

item.title: Why We All Need Sociology
item.description:
Social Life

Why We All Need Sociology

Understanding ourselves means understanding the society we live in.

Posted August 19, 2026

Key points
  • Modern sociology is criticized for supporting diversity, equity, inclusion, and other liberal programs.
  • It is crucial then to restate sociology’s quest to study the patterns, problems, and prospects of societies.
  • Humans are situated in contexts that include identity, relationships, groups, institutions, and societies.
  • Self-awareness—and personal freedom—depend on understanding those settings,

Last month, the Wall Street Journal published an article asking whether it is now time to “liquidate” sociology, the academic study of human societies. As many readers know, charges of this sort have become common recently. Conspicuous in this regard are the actions of the governor and legislature of Florida, which removed sociology as a core curriculum requirement in its state university system.

Sociology, some argue, has been the primary source for public commitments to diversity, equity, and inclusion. It has championed rights for historically mistreated groups like racial and ethnic minorities, women, and gay people. According to detractors, sociologists are overly sensitive to the challenges faced by immigrants, the poor, people accused of crimes, and the disabled. The broader public, critics conclude, does not wish to be morally aroused in this way.

At a time like this, it’s important to explain why sociology remains important, not just as a legitimate focus of scientific investigation but as a key part of people’s general education. This is especially critical in a country like the United States, which tends to champion individual, even psychological, accounts of the human condition.

Many readers have taken sociology courses in school and have their own understandings of that discipline. The rest should know that sociology is the study of the patterns, problems, and prospects of human relationships. If sociology has a credo, it is that people are profoundly influenced, even defined, by their involvement with other people. Those social connections are of different kinds and exist at different levels of “social structure.” To be human is to be set amidst these contexts.

Although sociology is mostly a descriptive and explanatory science—What causes crime rates to go up and down? How do population movements affect city services? Why do so many of us get divorced?—I restate here that sociologists also are interested in the problems of societies and in the possibilities for better ways of addressing these. Nearly 200 years ago, French philosopher Auguste Comte envisioned sociology as a “queen of the sciences” which comprehended and coordinated more specialized ways of studying human behavior. Might there be “laws” of social functioning? Can the good society be “engineered”?

Few sociologists today support Comte’s grand vision. However, most take their responsibilities seriously and do more than describe social patterns. In the U.S., sociology departments arose during the Progressive Era of the early 20th century, and sociology has always been more popular during liberal decades like the 1960s. To be sure, there have been conservative sociologists, including some who advocated Social Darwinism. But Progressivism remains a dominant commitment for most who practice that discipline.

Whatever one’s political or moral inclinations, why should any of us study sociology, or at least think in sociological terms? Consider below some of the levels of social structure I mentioned above.

Self or identity

Fundamental to sociology is the idea that people are comprehended in terms of socially recognized designations or “labels.” Many of these identity tags we ourselves accept as key features of who we are. Pointedly, those designations—being tall, from New Jersey, good at pickleball, employed at a grocery store, and so forth—only have meaning because they locate us in a specific universe of people. Some people share our trait; others don’t. At any rate, we operate socially and experience the world as collections of these identity referents.

Psychologists focus more on personality traits, our individual tendencies to think, feel, and behave in certain ways. Sociologists stress the impact of public descriptions and the fact that people commonly reject the labels others give them.

Interpersonal relationships

However important our individual thoughts and behaviors may be, we do not create our lives through private assertions. We live “in company” with others. Such people check our more unusual impulses; they give us our values; they protect us and grant us status; they provide places to work and rest. At best, they love and nurture us.

Psychologists emphasize our own experiences in these relationships—perhaps with friends, family members, or work colleagues. Sociologists stress the character of those relationships instead. To what extent are current difficulties the result of patterns that other people shape as much as we do?

Groups and organizations

Families are not collections of one-on-one relationships. Neither is that book club nor Thursday poker game we belong to. Instead, groups are entities of their own sorts. They have histories, membership criteria, and rules for operation. They have ranking systems and procedures for disciplining their members. Like individuals, they begin, grow, dwindle, and die.

Ordinarily larger and more abstract, organizations are formal frameworks for human participation. Some exist as vast, transpersonal (even transnational) bureaucracies with sharply defined goals, rules, roles, and chains of command. Commonly, sociologists are thought of as people who study these schools, churches, military units, hospitals, businesses, labor unions, and the like. Inevitably, such inquiries lead to ideas about how such units might be organized differently.

Social institutions

Every society confronts basic issues pertinent to human survival and establishes ways of responding to these. In that light, economies provide needed goods and services, governments regulate issues of social protection and coordination, families manage domestic life and child development. There are systems addressing healthcare, education, religion, and recreation as well. Commonly, these patterns exist as society-wide frameworks. They are enforced by laws and customs and given stability by thousands of organizations that operate on those terms.

Pointedly, the task of sociology is to study these vast, historically shifting arrangements, to point out problematic elements, and to suggest modifications to those lifeways. Not surprisingly, sociology’s detractors see these recommendations as disruptive and impertinent.

Community and society

Historically, people have lived together geographically, in physically situated places where they conduct their rounds of existence. Each day features hundreds of encounters with similarly located others, as we travel to schools, jobs, stores, medical centers, and the like. We think of ourselves as living in neighborhoods, communities, cities, and countries; and those identities may be reinforced by governmental regulations.

In such circumstances of shared living, all the above levels of social structure come into play. Other local people—perhaps the hardware store clerk or dentist—make our accustomed way of life possible. The sociologist’s task is to describe these communities, with their distinctive mixes of occupations, social classes, ethnic identities, religions, and beliefs.

It is said that our online, highly traveled world is destroying those old confinements of “place.” New communities—featuring new interests and loyalties—are emerging. Understanding those new alignments is also sociology’s task.

Sociology will and should have its critics, particularly if the historic commitments of the discipline become too narrowly focused and moral philosophizing overwhelms patient analysis. But all of us should be clear that an absence of sociology means a society without far-reaching institutional analysis, where the deeper meanings of our collective life go unexamined. In a worst-case scenario, poorly informed individuals stand naked before hugely configured, powerful organizations of government and business. Populations retreat into the forms of privatism these organizations permit. In counterpoint, sociology’s purpose is to educate people about better possibilities for living.
